column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Whoever relieves a believer of one of the distresses of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection;

whoever makes things easy for someone in hardship, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter; whoever conceals [the faults of] a Muslim, Allah will conceal [his faults] in this world and the Hereafter. Allah helps the servant as long as the servant helps his brother.

Whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah will make easy for him thereby a path to Paradise. No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, except that tranquillity descends upon them,

mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him. And whoever is held back by his deeds will not be hastened forward by his lineage.” Reported by Muslim with this wording.

His words, “Whoever relieves a believer of one of the distresses of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection”: kurbah (distress) is hardship and straits, and relieving it (tanfīs) is removing it.

The recompense for relieving a distress in this world is that one of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection is relieved for him. The recompense is of the same kind as the deed, and there is no doubt that here the recompense is greater,
because of the severity of the distresses of the Day of Resurrection and how great the benefit is to the distressed in having them relieved.

His words, “whoever makes things easy for someone in hardship, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter”: here too the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, the deed being easing things for one in hardship,

by helping him to remove his hardship. If he is in debt, one helps him by giving him the means to pay off his debt; and if the debt is owed to oneself, one grants him respite, if one does not release him from it altogether—and releasing him is better than granting respite,

because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And if someone is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until ease; but if you give it as charity, it is better for you, if only you knew” [al-Baqarah 2:280]. He ﷺ made clear that the recompense for easing is an easing that comes in this world and the Hereafter.

His words, “whoever conceals [the faults of] a Muslim, Allah will conceal [his faults] in this world and the Hereafter”: here too the deed is concealing in this world, and the recompense for it is concealing in this world and the Hereafter. Concealing is hiding a fault and not exposing it.

Someone who is known for uprightness and falls into a sin is advised and his fault concealed. But when someone is known for corruption and criminality, concealing his fault may make his crime seem trivial to him, so that he persists in it and goes further. In such a case the benefit lies in not concealing it,
so that he receives the punishment that deters him from returning to his crime and aggression.
His words, “Allah helps the servant as long as the servant helps his brother”, urge the Muslim to help his Muslim brother,
and show that whenever he helps his brothers, he thereby gains the help and guidance of Allah. It is one of the comprehensive statements of the Messenger ﷺ.

His words, “Whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah will make easy for him thereby a path to Paradise”, urge seeking knowledge of the Sharīʿah and taking the paths that lead to acquiring it, whether by travelling to seek it

or by taking the means of acquiring it: obtaining beneficial books, reading them and benefiting from them, keeping the company of scholars and learning from them, and so on. The recompense for this from Allah is making easy the path by which the student of knowledge reaches Paradise,
by helping him to attain what he sought, so that he acquires knowledge, and also by helping him to act on the rulings of the Sharīʿah he has learned, which leads him to enter Paradise.
His words, “No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it together, except that tranquillity descends upon them, mercy covers them,

the angels surround them, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him”: the houses of Allah are the mosques, and their attribution to Allah is an attribution of honour. The mosques are the most beloved places to Allah,

because he ﷺ said: “The most beloved places to Allah are its mosques, and the most hateful places to Allah are its markets.” Reported by Muslim (671). The hadith urges gathering in the mosques to recite the Qurʾān and study it.

This may be by one of those gathered reciting while the rest listen, or by their reciting in turn so that they correct one another's recitation, each benefiting from the others in improving his recitation and correcting mistakes, if there are any. If there is someone among them who knows its tafsīr, he teaches them;

and if they are people of knowledge in it, they study its meanings together, referring in that to the books of tafsīr, both narration-based and reasoning-based, built on what the Salaf of this nation were upon.

The recompense for gathering in the mosques to recite and study the Qurʾān is four things: tranquillity and calm descend upon them; mercy covers them, that is, envelops and enfolds them; the angels surround them, that is, encircle them; and Allah the Exalted mentions them before the angels.

His words, “And whoever is held back by his deeds will not be hastened forward by his lineage”, mean: if a person's deeds hold him back from entering Paradise, his lineage will not hasten him into Paradise,

because what counts in this is faith and taqwā, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:13]. Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (2/308): “It means that it is deeds that bring the servant to the ranks of the Hereafter,

as the Exalted said: ‘And for all there are ranks according to what they did’ [al-Anʿām 6:132]. If a person's deeds are too slow to bring him to the high stations with Allah the Exalted, his lineage will not hasten him on to reach those ranks,

for Allah has made the recompense depend on deeds, not on lineage, as the Exalted said: ‘So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no lineage among them that Day, nor will they ask about one another’ [al-Muʾminūn 23:101].” He went on to say: “On this meaning one of them says:
By your life, a man is nothing but his religion, / so do not abandon taqwā, relying on lineage.
Islam raised Salmān of Persia, / and shirk brought low the noble-born Abū Lahab.”
Relieving distresses in this world is encouraged, and in return Allah the Exalted relieves the distresses of the Day of Resurrection.
The recompense is of the same kind as the deed: the deed is relieving a distress, and the recompense is relieving a distress.
Making things easy for those in hardship is encouraged, and its recompense is ease in this world and the Hereafter.
Concealing faults is encouraged when the benefit lies in concealing them, and its recompense is concealment in this world and the Hereafter.
The Muslim is urged to help his Muslim brother; whenever he helps his brothers, he thereby gains the help and guidance of Allah.
The hadith shows the merit of seeking knowledge of the Sharīʿah.
The hadith shows the merit of gathering in the mosques to recite and study the Qurʾān.
Faith and righteous deeds are the cause of entering Paradise and attaining high ranks with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Noble lineage without righteous deeds does not benefit its owner with Allah.
